questions.stem: Shawn, 75, has COPD and is breathless in ED on 2 L/min nasal prongs. As part of your focused examination you want to check for a CO2 retention flap, because his oxygen needs careful titration. Which instruction to Shawn best elicits this sign?
options: "Hold your arms out in front, palms up, and close your eyes for me and hold still."
"Touch your nose, then my finger, as quickly as you can, a few times."
"Arms straight out, bend your wrists back, spread your fingers and hold."
"Squeeze my two fingers as hard as you can with both hands, and let go."
questions.why: A CO2 retention flap (asterixis) shows when the wrists are held dorsiflexed with the fingers spread: the sustained posture briefly lapses, giving a flapping movement. Hold the position for about 30 seconds.
notes: This tests for pronator drift, a sign of an upper motor neurone lesion, not a hypercapnic flap.
Finger-nose testing looks for cerebellar ataxia and intention tremor, not asterixis.
Grip strength tests power. A flap needs a sustained posture with the wrists bent back, not a squeeze.

questions.stem: Shawn, 75, with an infective exacerbation of COPD, has had repeated salbutamol and ipratropium, prednisolone and amoxicillin, with oxygen titrated to SpO2 88 to 92%. A repeat ABG at 1 hour shows pH 7.29 and PaCO2 66 mmHg. He is alert and can protect his airway. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start bilevel non-invasive ventilation in a monitored area
Increase the oxygen to target SpO2 94 to 98% by Hudson mask
Give an IV aminophylline loading dose over 20 minutes
Start CPAP at 10 cm H2O by full face mask
questions.why: Acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH below 7.35, PaCO2 above 45 mmHg) that persists despite optimal medical treatment is the indication for bilevel NIV. Inspiratory pressure support increases ventilation and clears CO2. Escalate to ICU if he deteriorates or cannot tolerate it.
notes: More oxygen in a CO2 retainer worsens hypercapnia and acidosis. The target stays at 88 to 92%.
Aminophylline adds little benefit and has significant toxicity in COPD exacerbations. It does not replace ventilatory support for acidosis.
CPAP gives no inspiratory pressure support, so it does little to clear CO2. Bilevel NIV is the mode for hypercapnic COPD.

questions.stem: Shawn, 75, has compensated chronic hypercapnia (PaCO2 52 mmHg, HCO3 29 mmol/L). A clinician puts him on a high-flow mask. His SpO2 rises to 98% but he becomes drowsy as his PaCO2 climbs. What is the main mechanism behind this rise in PaCO2?
options: Abolition of the hypoxic drive, so central respiratory drive stops altogether
Oxygen-induced bronchospasm, which raises airway resistance and the work of breathing
Higher CO2 production as metabolic rate rises with better tissue oxygen delivery
Release of hypoxic vasoconstriction, so blood goes to poorly ventilated alveoli
questions.why: High FiO2 reverses hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. Blood then perfuses poorly ventilated units, which worsens V/Q mismatch and effective dead space. Together with the Haldane effect, this raises PaCO2 more than any loss of hypoxic drive does.
notes: Minute ventilation falls only a little with oxygen and does not stop. Loss of hypoxic drive is a minor contributor, not the main mechanism.
Oxygen does not cause bronchospasm. Airway resistance in his exacerbation comes from inflammation and bronchoconstriction.
Extra oxygen does not meaningfully raise CO2 production. The problem is CO2 elimination, not production.

questions.stem: Shawn, 75, needs a repeat arterial blood gas from his right radial artery an hour after starting treatment in ED. You palpate the pulse at the wrist, just proximal to the flexor retinaculum, before inserting the needle. Where does the radial artery lie at this site?
options: Between the flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus tendons, beside the median nerve
Just lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon, over the distal radius
Just lateral to the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, beside the pisiform
Deep in the anatomical snuffbox, on the scaphoid and trapezium
questions.why: At the distal forearm the radial artery runs just lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon, lying on the distal radius. The bone underneath lets you compress it after the puncture. Check ulnar collateral flow (modified Allen test) first.
notes: The median nerve lies here, so a puncture at this site risks nerve injury rather than reaching the artery.
This is where the ulnar artery and nerve lie, not the radial artery.
The radial artery does pass through the snuffbox, but that is distal to this site and is not where an ABG is usually taken.
